Hi, from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly. Federal agents have searched the
Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota in an ongoing investigation
into allegations related to immigration fraud. NPR's Barbara Sprunt says Omar has been a
sharp critic and frequent target of President Trump.
The Department of Justice says agents with Homeland Security investigations were executing
a judicially authorized search warrant and that it's part of an ongoing federal criminal
investigation. A spokesperson for the Congresswoman calls the search a "outrageous abuse of power"
and an "unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political
enemies." The search took place ahead of next month's midterm elections in which Omar is
seeking re-election. Vice President Vance has previously alleged Omar committed immigration
fraud, something she denies. Barbara Sprunt, NPR News, Washington.
Russia continues to attack energy facilities in Ukraine despite President Trump's assertion
that the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire. Ukraine's president, Volodomir
Zelensky, says he supports such a truce, but only if Moscow halts its attacks. NPR's Charles
Maines is in Moscow.
Ukraine is for a deal if it includes an end to Russian attacks on energy, heating and
electrical facilities. But without that, Trump is essentially asking Ukraine to give up one
of the few real leverage points it has against a more powerful adversary. Meanwhile, Russia's
long-held position is that anything less than a comprehensive peace deal, such as, for example,
a ceasefire, is an opportunity for Ukraine to regroup and rearm. Russia is interested
in pressing its current leverage in missiles and drones to the maximum, particularly as
we enter the winter months with Ukraine's air defenses depleted.
It's NPR's Charles Maines. Australia's government says it opposes the Pentagon's plan to livestream
the December execution of a former U.S. Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort
Hood, Texas. The 2009 attack also left more than 30 others injured. As Kristina Kukla
reports from Melbourne, Australia's prime minister is urging social media companies
not to share the footage.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government has sought advice on what
it can do to block the livestream of the Fort Hood shooters' execution by firing squad.
Speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, Albanese issued a warning to social media
platforms.
I'm making it very clear to them right now that as far as I'm concerned, this has no
place in our countries.
Australia's online safety regulator says it doesn't have the power to stop the livestream,
but would monitor if sites are complying with regulations requiring them to protect users
from harmful material. This comes as parliamentarians across the Australian political divide call
for the livestream to be banned, echoing the bipartisan backlash in the U.S.
For NPR News, I'm Kristina Kukla in Melbourne.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Jury selection is scheduled to begin today in the federal trial of the man charged with
killing 10 people at a grocery store in Buffalo, New York. That shooting occurred four years
ago at the top's friendly market. Peyton Gendrone is facing more than two dozen federal counts,
mostly federal hate crimes charges. Prosecutors have described the 23-year-old as a white
supremacist who targeted black people in the shooting. He's currently serving a life sentence
after pleading guilty to state murder charges. Defense attorneys say they're hoping to prevent
Gendrone from pacing the death penalty if he's convicted.
Police and park operator Six Flags says it's temporarily closing nine of its roller coasters
at a half dozen parks across the U.S. This follows the death of a person who fell from
a coaster yesterday at Six Flags over Georgia, near Atlanta. Melissa Fato with member station
WABE has more.
Footage from multiple local media outlets shows park staff evacuating riders from the
lift hill of Goliath. The 200-foot hyper coaster opened in 2006. Cobb County police confirmed
several others are injured and the department is investigating the incident. The Six Flags
chain has seen financial challenges and leadership changes since it merged with its once-competitor
Cedar Fair in 2024. This incident comes on the heels of Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern
California announcing it's retiring its famous fourth-dimension coaster, X2. Amid allegations,
it has caused several riders serious brain injuries. For NPR News, I'm Melissa Fato in
Atlanta.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.
